correctness.rationale: Quadratic exactness is equivalent to the moment-vector hull event. A point strictly interior to the hull yields positive weights on all sample nodes by mixing any representation with uniform positive weights. Convexity of the parabola gives the necessary-and-sufficient nearest-product and extreme-product inequalities; their failure events are disjoint. Joint extreme and nearest-point density integrals yield the exact p_m formula with correct boundary terms. Laurent-power integration yields rational plus rational log3 at every m. Endpoint Laplace contributions are 1/2 and 3/2, so the total sharp failure prefactor is 1+2=3; the other contribution decays at rate no greater than (1-1/sqrt3)^m. A positive-series rational enclosure for log3 certifies the first 95% threshold m=11. The included exact-rational checker passes 4500 independent geometric comparisons plus finite algebraic/numerical checks; infinite conclusions rest on the proof.

originality.rationale: The existing three-node probability agrees exactly with the m=3 specialization and is explicitly excluded from novelty. The distinct claim is an all-integer probability identity, a sharp three-times-(2/3)^m failure prefactor and the resulting exact 95%-success threshold. The motivating 2026 preprint proves broad existence/weight-box estimates, not this exact distribution. The inspected open-access 2023 random-convex-hull paper gives general inclusion bounds and cubature applications rather than an exact uniform-parabola law. Semantic searches found no statement subsuming the all-m identity and leading constant. General earlier random-polytope/moment-curve literature remains a real priority risk; lack of hits is not a proof of uniqueness.
residual_risks: An older general formula for convex hulls of i.i.d. points on convex curves might imply the same all-m identity, even without mentioning quadrature.

value.rationale: Sampling positive quadratic-exact rules is the central probabilistic-quadrature problem in the motivating literature. Exact success probabilities for every sample budget, a rigorously minimal m=11 for 95% success, and the separation of extreme-node and nearest-node failure mechanisms directly inform sample-size design. The asymptotic prefactor 3 is not supplied by generic success-probability bounds and reflects two endpoint contributions. The result is a natural complete finite-sample classification rather than a changed constant in the prior three-node result; no broad numerical-analysis extension is asserted.
